subject: Grouping replicates to increase sample size

messages.author: 00ce423c0ff05c01
messages.subject: Grouping replicates to increase sample size
parts:
I am surveying small carnivores in Mongolia using line transects and
spotlighting from a truck and am new to Distance surveys. I have low
sample sizes and would like to group seasonal replicates to increase
sample size. I carry out a 56km transect consisting of 8 separate line
transects every week, producing 12-13 weekly samples per 3 month
season. Can I group data per season to increase sample sizes, for
example I generally see 5 corsac foxes per survey, can I use the data
from all 13 surveys per season (roughly 60-65 sightings) to estimate
density? Does anyone have any advice about this issue.

Steve Ross

messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: Grouping replicates to increase sample size
parts:
Hi Steve, list,

Enter the data into distance as 8 samples (lines) each of length (line
length*number of visits). So, for a 7km line visited 12 times in a season,
enter this as a 84km line. All the observations for that line go in the
observation layer, as if you had surveyed an 84km line once. Otherwise, the
analysis proceeds as usual.

Note that 8 is a rather small sample size of lines. You would be better to do
fewer temporal replicates over more lines - especially since in your habitat,
which I guess is Mongolian plains, it's relatively easy to drive where you
like. You really want at least 20-30 - but if it is equally easy to sample a
new line as it is to drive down an old one, then do a new line each time. If
you sample 96 lines is a 3-month season, then a good design would be a
systematic grid of 96 7km lines placed throughout your study area - see
Advanced Distance Sampling figure 7.8 for an example. This kind of design can
be created using the survey design module in Distance. Another good design is
a circuit design, where the transect is (say) a square (see Fig 7.3 of
Introduction to Distance sampling). That way you can start at any convenient
point on the square, and you end up where you started. Disadvantages of this
design are: (i) you may chase animals away from the start point, so get a
biased sample as you come back to it at the end of the survey, or you may move
animals around the square ahead of you; (ii) such designs can't be created
(yet) in Distance -- although you could always generate a systematic grid of
points in Distance and then superimpose the squares on a map by hand.

If you do create many more lines, you'll probably want to visit them in a
systematic manner if possible, to guard against any large-scale movement of
animals through the study area within the 3 month season. So (if logistically
possible -- ie study area not too large) you might visit lines 1, 9, 17, ...
first, then lines 2, 10, 18, ... etc etc.

Hope this helps,

- Len
